Advertisement Advertisement Read also: Airlines face a December 31 biometric cliff as yuletide peak collides with vPASS mandate The continent processed 1.83 trillion instant payment transactions in 2025, down from 1.99 trillion in 2024, according to the 2026 State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems in Africa (SIIPS) study, which tracks the development and use of real-time payment infrastructure across African markets. The decline reversed a period of sustained growth in transaction volumes, which rose from 1.18 trillion in 2021 to 1.50 trillion in 2022, 1.81 trillion in 2023 and a peak of 1.99 trillion in 2024. Mobile money and cross-domain payment systems accounted for much of the contraction. Mobile money transactions fell to 469 billion in 2025 from 523 billion a year earlier, while cross-domain transactions declined to 1.22 trillion from 1.35 trillion. Read also: Offshore funds face rationing as Dangote Refinery expands N6trn IPO to shield retail buyers Advertisement Bank-based instant payment systems, however, recorded growth, with transactions increasing to 139 billion from 116 billion in 2024. The segment has expanded steadily over five years, rising from 66 billion transactions in 2021. Despite the decline in overall volumes, mobile money remained the dominant channel, accounting for 73 percent of instant payment transactions in 2025. Advertisement The slowdown comes amid persistent concerns about fraud, transaction failures and consumer confidence, with the study indicating that the reliability of payment systems and the ability to recover lost funds are increasingly important to adoption. About 41 percent of surveyed digital payment users said they had experienced a fraudulent transaction, with individuals and micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) reporting broadly similar exposure. Advertisement Advertisement Read also: Arik Air plans 2027 fleet expansion as jet fuel prices ease after Middle East shock Fraud levels varied across markets. Among individual users, 37 percent in the Central African Economic and Monetary Community (CEMAC) region reported experiencing fraud, compared with 28 percent in Morocco. Among businesses, the incidence was higher in South Africa, where 56 percent reported fraud, and in CEMAC, at 51 percent. The consequences of fraud extended beyond financial losses, affecting how users engage with digital payment services. About 43 percent of respondents who lost money to fraud reduced their use of digital payments, while 20 percent of those whose funds were recovered through reversals or refunds increased their usage. The findings suggest that the speed and effectiveness of dispute resolution and reimbursement mechanisms could influence adoption, as users weigh the convenience of digital transactions against the risks of losing money. Operational challenges also remain widespread. Nearly half of surveyed individuals and MSMEs had experienced at least one problem involving failed, delayed or duplicated transactions, or payments sent to the wrong recipient. In Rwanda, 78 percent of MSMEs reported delayed transactions, while Nigeria recorded high levels of failed and duplicate payments among both individuals and businesses. South Africa reported comparatively fewer operational problems among individual users and MSMEs. The findings highlight the challenges facing payment providers and regulators as they seek to expand digital financial services, particularly in markets where instant payment systems are increasingly used for everyday transactions, business payments and transfers. The study also identified artificial intelligence as an emerging tool in fraud prevention, noting that financial service providers were adopting AI-based monitoring systems more widely and faster than instant payment system operators. It recommends stronger cooperation in sharing fraud intelligence, improved identity verification systems and clearer mechanisms for users to dispute transactions, arguing that greater reliability and accountability are essential to sustaining confidence in digital payment infrastructure.
